nameStory: The "hog-peanut" name comes from the underground seeds this clever vine produces, which wild hogs and other animals love to dig up and eat. These buried "peanuts" aren't true peanuts at all, but they're just as nutritious and were an important food source for Native Americans too.
description: American hog-peanut is a slender, twining vine that climbs up through shrubs and other plants in shady woodlands. This annual to perennial member of the legume family can scramble 3-6 feet high, wrapping its delicate stems around whatever support it finds. Like other legumes, it produces small pea-like flowers and has three-leaflet leaves, but what makes it truly special is its ability to produce two completely different types of seeds.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three heart-shaped leaflets per leaf, each about 1-3 inches long with a soft, slightly fuzzy texture. The leaflets are arranged like clover leaves and turn easily in your fingers when you touch them.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny pale pink to white pea-like flowers hang in small clusters from the leaf joints. Each flower is only about 1/4 inch long and has the typical legume flower shape with a banner petal on top.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Delicate twining vine that spirals counterclockwise around stems and branches. The thin, slightly hairy stems feel flexible and break easily if pulled too hard.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces two types of seeds: small flat pods above ground from the flowers, and special underground seeds near the base that look like tiny beans buried in the soil.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thin, wiry stems covered in fine hairs that feel slightly rough when you run your finger along them. The stems are green to reddish-brown and rarely thicker than a pencil.

habitat: Look for American hog-peanut in rich, moist deciduous and mixed woodlands throughout New England, especially in areas with partial shade. It thrives in the understory of maple, oak, and beech forests, often climbing through shrubs like elderberry and dogwood along woodland edges and stream banks.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge in late spring with their characteristic three-leaflet leaves, beginning to twine up through surrounding vegetation as the forest canopy fills in.
seasonality.summer: Blooms from mid to late summer with small pink-white flowers, while simultaneously developing its underground seeds at the base of the plant.
seasonality.fall: Above-ground seed pods mature and split open in early fall, while underground seeds can be found by gently digging near the base before the vine dies back.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to the ground, leaving only the buried seeds to survive until next growing season.

funFact: This vine is like a botanical hedge fund investor - it produces two completely different types of seeds as insurance! The underground seeds never see sunlight and are produced in special buried flowers that never open, guaranteeing local reproduction even if the above-ground flowers fail.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with wild bean vines, but hog-peanut has much smaller flowers and its distinctive underground seeds. Remember: if you can dig up bean-like seeds near the base of a delicate three-leaflet vine, you've found your hog-peanut!
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name, hog-peanut is completely unrelated to true peanuts (which are actually legumes that grow underground in a different way). The "ground bean" alternative name is more accurate, as this plant is genuinely related to beans and produces its underground seeds through a fascinating process called cleistogamy.
compareHints: American hog-peanut is the only species in its genus found in New England, making it unique among our native vines. Compared to other legume vines like wild bean or groundnut, hog-peanut is much more delicate with smaller flowers and the distinctive underground seed production that sets it apart from all other climbing legumes in our region.
